extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, and clients seeking Australian patent attorney advice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing and overcoming novelty and inventive step objections under the Patents Act 1990 (Cth) in Australia, with practical pointers for claim drafting, prosecution and litigation. Focuses on how the statutory tests and case law are applied during examination, opposition and revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (absolute newness)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is patentable only if it is novel; an invention lacks novelty if all of its essential features are disclosed in a single piece of prior art information forming part of the prior art base before the priority date (Sections 7(1) and 18(1)(b) of the Patents Act 1990 (Cth)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is assessed claim-by-claim and focuses on what the claim requires, not the general idea. The prior art base is broad (any information publicly available anywhere by written publication, oral disclosure, use or other act). Establishing novelty often involves amending claims to more precisely define and distinguish the invention from known material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art base (scope of what counts as prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'prior art base' in Australia includes any information made publicly available anywhere in the world before the priority date — written publications, oral disclosures, use, or any other act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the wide ambit of the prior art base, examiners and opponents may rely on diverse sources. Practitioners must consider worldwide disclosures when assessing novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation / 'reverse infringement' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty (anticipation) is assessed by asking whether carrying out what is disclosed in a prior art disclosure would necessarily fall within the scope of the claim (the 'reverse infringement' principle as in General Tire & Rubber Co v Firestone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires more than resemblance or overlap; the prior art must disclose all essential features of the claim in a clear, unequivocal and complete manner. Case law (Nicaro Holdings v Martin Engineering; Asahi Kasei) emphasises reading the disclosure through the eyes of the person skilled in the art and whether the disclosure enables putting the invention into practice. Ambiguous, incomplete or requiring further invention disclosures do not necessarily destroy novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed feature that is an inevitable result of performing what is already known can defeat novelty even if that feature was not recognized or expressly described previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in chemical and pharmaceutical contexts: a newly identified mechanism of action for a known compound will not confer novelty if that mechanism inevitably occurred whenever the compound was administered. New insight into an old act does not make the act itself new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole of contents novelty (earlier Australian filings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Australian 'whole of contents' provision allows novelty to be objected to based on the information contained in earlier Australian patent applications, even if those earlier applications were not published at the relevant priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision aims to prevent two patents for the same invention. It operates strictly for novelty (not for inventive step). When raised, detailed analysis and careful comparison of disclosures and claim scope is required, as minor differences can be decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's own conduct: public disclosure and secret use
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's pre-filing public disclosures (presentations, publications, sales, online disclosures) form part of the prior art base and will generally destroy novelty; secret commercial exploitation before the priority date can be a ground for invalidity under Section 18(1)(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited statutory grace periods may apply but are narrow. Secret use exceptions (e.g., reasonable trial and experiment) are narrowly construed and very fact-specific. Applicants should manage disclosure carefully to avoid self-destruction of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (non-obviousness) statutory test
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if it is not obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art in light of: (a) the common general knowledge in that field; and (b) certain prior art information that the skilled person could reasonably be expected to have ascertained, understood and regarded as relevant (Section 7(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike novelty, inventive step permits consideration of multiple sources of information and combinations of documents, provided statutory criteria for combining those sources are satisfied. The assessment is fact- and evidence-driven and often contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (skilled addressee construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'person skilled in the art' is a hypothetical person with ordinary technical knowledge and skills but no inventive capacity, used as the benchmark for assessing inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construct injects an element of objectivity but the assessment retains subjectivity in defining the skilled person's common general knowledge and what they would reasonably have ascertained. Arguments focus on what that person would have done or combined at the priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cripps question / 'led as a matter of course' test
rubrics_metrics.description: A guiding test for inventive step (from Aktiebolaget Hässle v Alphapharm): would a skilled person, faced with the problem the invention solves, have been 'led directly as a matter of course to try the claimed invention in the expectation that it might well produce a solution'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a hindsight 'obvious to try' test; it asks whether the path to the invention was straightforward and predictable. Demonstrating that the invention was not a predictable routine choice supports inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem identification as a basis for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step can reside in identifying the correct technical problem to be solved; if prior art failed to recognise the true nature of the problem, recognising it can support inventive step (Wellcome Foundation v VR Laboratories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the invention arises from a non-obvious insight into the problem rather than merely from an obvious solution. Emphasise differences in how the problem was framed compared with prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary indicators / objective evidence of non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary or 'commercial' indicators that support inventive step include satisfying a long-felt need, evidence that others tried and failed, significant commercial success, and copying by competitors (as recognised in Winner v Ammar Holdings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and present documentary and factual evidence (industry recognition, failed attempts by others, licensing, sales data, instances of copying) to bolster arguments that an invention was not obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting and disclosure management as strategic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective patent protection depends on disciplined disclosure management and precise claim drafting to navigate novelty and inventive step objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with objections, amend and refine claims to distinguish over prior art, frame the technical problem and advantages clearly, and use evidence and secondary indicators where available. Seek professional advice to turn examination objections into opportunities to strengthen the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and interplay between novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty and inventive step are distinct but complementary legal gates: novelty asks whether the claimed subject-matter is absolutely new; inventive step asks whether it would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure on either ground is fatal to patentability. Legal strategy must address both: securing clear differences from single-piece disclosures for novelty, and demonstrating non-obviousness (including via combinations, skilled person analysis, Cripps question and secondary indicators) for inventive step.
